Do you like Haruki Murakami's writing?
I grew up on Japanese media, so I only find it natural that I'd understand and enjoy Murakami's writing.

I bought The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle when it came out and was absolutely blown away. There were times where I'd put the book down and just stare at nothing, trying to process the beauty of the passage I just read. I don't know if spending 10 years of my childhood in Japan had any impact on how much I liked it.

I loved that book. On the other hand, I haven't been bothered to read through much more of his work. I don't know why.

Murakami is a bit of an anomaly to me. I both love and absolutely hate his writing. He has a manner of writing that isn't particularly floral or unique at first glance, yet manifests into a completely visceral reading experience. He's stated that words are merely tools to him. I respect a degree of brevity in a writer, and I think it speaks to his ability as an author to evoke emotion at such a raw level. But, I often hate his work for what I assume is a cultural barrier that interjects throughout his stories (I'm assuming, because I see this element in more japanese media than western, and I'm not quite accustomed to asian media). For example, in Norwegian Wood, when Midori explains how she sits naked in front of a picture of her dead father and shows him her vagina. Yeah... not gonna be able to get through that passage without cringing (no pun intended). He also has the most tropes of any author I've read. His protagonists can come across as passive and limp-wristed. And yet, despite all of this, there is something nebulous about Murakami's writing that has me returning to his novels repeatedly.

I started out with his short stories and thought they were brilliant (Blind Willow Sleeping Woman) because they captured perfectly the strangeness of certain small moments in life (even if the writing was a little heavy handed at times). In particular, I loved the short story that eventually became the Wind Up Bird Chronicles (The Windup Bird and Tuesday's Women). I transitioned to his novels and found that the magic of his short stories was completely ruined for me. The novels feel aimless, and weird for weird's sake, and just drag on forever. I left reading them thinking "what was the point of all that?". I purposefully avoided reading Norwegian Wood because I didn't want to ruin my earlier memory of the short story this was based on.

I've read Hard-Boiled Wonderland and the End of the World and The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle. It is difficult for me to tell whether or not he deserves the level of appreciation I gave those books, however. A lot of what I love about his work is it's originality and the quirk of the writing style, descriptions, and characters. I'm not very wapanese, so for all I know his books could be super trope-ridden strings of cliches and colloquialisms. But either way, I really do enjoy reading him, even if he can be a bit hard to follow at times.

I just finished reading A Wild Sheep Chase. I have to say that I do indeed like his writing, but it is necessary to understand/familiarize oneself with the context of his works, namely Japanese society and culture. Then, his stories become so much more profound and understandable.
I read a book of his. I like his voice.
I love Murakami. In my opinion he's the best writer of our time. "The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle " is by far my favorite book. Reading it feels like drifting into a dream without realizing it.
